analysis.one_liner: Opens most of the outer Continental Shelf to oil and gas drilling and rolls back environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 106 House Republicans, sat in committee and never received a House floor vote before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have reopened vast areas of the federal waters off the Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf coasts to oil and gas leasing. Areas 50 to 100 miles from shore would have opened by default unless a state's legislature voted to block drilling, the President's authority to protect areas would have been sharply limited, and seismic surveys and other early drilling work would have been exempted from environmental review. In return, coastal states would have received a large share of federal drilling royalties, 37.5% rising to 75% near shore, to spend on schools, tax cuts, infrastructure, and coastal projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain access to huge new tracts of public ocean acreage, with relaxed environmental review, royalty relief provisions, a requirement that the government offer 75% of unleased acreage in each planning area, and a new right for leaseholders denied permits to make the government buy their leases back. Coastal state and local governments gain a large new stream of royalty money. Petroleum and mining engineering schools gain federal funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies and coastal states

how_it_helps.text: Opens Atlantic, Pacific, and eastern Gulf areas 50 to 100 miles from shore to oil and gas leasing unless a state petitions within a set deadline to keep them closed, and revokes the 1998 presidential withdrawal that protected many of those areas [S3].
Requires the Interior Secretary to offer at least 75% of available unleased acreage in each offshore planning area for lease in every five-year leasing program [S3].
Exempts lease suspensions and all preliminary offshore activities, including seismic testing, from environmental assessments and impact statements under the National Environmental Policy Act [S3].

Shares 37.5% of federal offshore drilling receipts with coastal states and local governments, rising to 75% for tracts near shore, usable for college tuition reduction, tax cuts, transportation, coastal restoration, or any other purpose under state law [S3].
Lets leaseholders whose permits were denied or delayed force the government to repurchase and cancel their leases, with compensation and a 10% penalty if the agency misses a 180-day deadline [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury loses royalty revenue that now goes to the general fund. Coastal communities and ocean users face new drilling, platforms, pipelines, and spill risk near their shores. The public bears weakened environmental review, since the bill categorically excludes early drilling activities and most later plans from study under the National Environmental Policy Act.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes areas 50 to 100 miles offshore open to drilling by default: a state must affirmatively petition to block leasing, and the Secretary must approve petitions unless leasing would probably cause serious harm, with approval automatic if the agency misses a 90-day deadline [S3].

It strips environmental review from the earliest and most intrusive phases of offshore exploration, categorically excluding seismic surveys and preliminary activities from any environmental assessment or impact statement [S3].

It limits the President to withdrawing no more than 25% of any planning area beyond 100 miles from shore, caps withdrawals at 10 years, and bars the President from undoing a state's choice to allow leasing [S3].

It penalizes future environmental protections: if a later federal law restricts offshore leasing or permitting, revenue sharing to the states automatically stops while the restriction lasts, and a lessee or producing state can trigger the determination [S3].
States receiving shared royalties would not have to account to the federal government for how they spend the money [S3].
New offshore leasing generally takes years to bring oil to market, so the bill's promise of relief at the gas pump, the political context of 2008, would have arrived long after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does contain real public benefits: a large, permanent royalty stream for coastal states and a dedicated wildlife and natural resources fund. But the core of the bill is a major expansion of drilling access on public waters bundled with weakened environmental review, default-open leasing rules, and lessee-friendly compensation rights. A fair reading is that the benefits to coastal governments were designed as the price for gaining their support for drilling, and the environmental and fiscal costs fall on the broader public. Anyone who values the existing review process and federal royalties would judge the trade as unfavorable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees and their subcommittees, a Republican member filed a petition to force it onto the floor, it never got the support needed, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Sue Myrick introduced the bill on May 21, 2008, and it was referred to the Natural Resources, Science and Technology, and Judiciary Committees [S5].
It was sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources and Energy and Environment subcommittees in late May and early June 2008, and no committee ever reported it out [S5].
On July 30, 2008, Rep. Jon Porter filed a discharge petition, a device to pull a bill out of committee and force a floor vote, but the bill never reached the floor [S5].
All 106 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].
Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, oil and gas companies did not gain access to the protected offshore areas, and the existing system of presidential withdrawals and environmental review stayed in place. Coastal communities faced no new drilling under the bill's default-open rules, and federal royalty money stayed with the Treasury rather than being redirected to states.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coasts and Treasury kept existing protections

sides.party_line_note: All 106 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic majority that controlled the House committees and floor calendar never gave the bill a vote.

industries.note: The bill hands companies access to vast new public offshore acreage, requires the government to offer 75% of unleased acreage in each planning area, relaxes royalty terms, and lets leaseholders force buyouts when permits are denied. The industry's gain comes at the cost of federal royalties and coastal environmental risk.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling, seismic, and pipeline contractors
industries.note: Mandated lease sales, categorical exclusion of seismic work from environmental review, and federal permitting of pipelines without state consent expand the market for exploration and construction services.

States and coastal counties would have received 37.5% to 75% of federal offshore drilling receipts, spendable on schools, tax cuts, infrastructure, or any purpose under state law, with no federal accounting required.

industries.industry: Oil shale and tar sands developers
industries.note: The bill repeals payment requirements for oil shale and tar sands leases and sets new royalty rules for those resources, lowering the cost of access to public onshore minerals.
The bill redirects federal funds to state-chartered petroleum and mining schools and creates scholarships and grants to train the energy industry's future workforce.

New platforms, seismic surveys, and pipeline construction near coasts would compete with fishing and tourism uses of the ocean, and the bill bars federal agencies from permitting uses incompatible with oil and gas production.
